In the case of international production companies, this rate can reach even higher. All respondents in the digital industry study pointed to the availability of skilled labour as a crucial factor behind their decision to launch an investment in Lower Silesia20. PRODUCT PERSONALISATION AND SERVITISATION The ability to create more product variants while using the same resources is crucial to building a competitive advantage. That’s why increasing production flexibility has long been a pressing matter for manufacturers. Again, data is the game-changer here. Processing real-time information at all stages of user interactions enables creating product simulations that can be adapted to match unique, individual requirements of the customer. Similarly, many manufacturing businesses now expand the value for their clients by shifting from selling products to selling Product-Service Systems (PSS). Pioneered in the 1960s by Rolls Royce, servitisation relieves customers of capital costs, instead offering them advanced solutions in a subscription model. 16 PLATFORMISATION OF PRODUCTION Just as products are now increasingly offered as a service, the manufacturing process is also subject to similar changes. ON INDUSTRY 4.0 WORLDWIDE Before the outbreak of COVID-19, there was widespread interest in Industry 4.0. The sector’s value was projected to grow up to $3.7 trillion by 20259. However, despite these positive outlooks, the actual landscape of Industry 4.0 adoption has been far more complex. ASPIRATIONS VS REALITY 90% of respondents in McKinsey’s10 annual survey admitted seeing the benefits of digital transformation in manufacturing. A majority of them included introducing new technologies as an essential part of their organisational development strategies. However, as research from the World Economic Forum11 demonstrates, despite these declarations, the reality was still far from this ideal. In 2018, the adoption of technology in production still remained slow across industries and regions. ip_data_security.text: This change wouldn’t be possible without advancements such as the Internet of Things (IoT), the Cloud, Robotic Process Automation (RPA), or Artificial Intelligence (AI). 13 Therefore, this publication follows the BCG’s definition of Industry 4.01, seeing it as a transformation that enables analysing data across machines and using it for more efficient manufacturing at reduced costs. CORE TECHNOLOGIES SUPPORTING INDUSTRY 4.0 Autonomous robots & cobots Digital Twins & simulation The AI-powered cloud Augmented & virtual reality Digital integration systems The Industrial Internet of Things Additive manufacturing Big Data & analytics Cybersecurity * ORGANISED AFTER THE BOSTON CONSUL TING GROUP Apart from increasing productivity, Industry 4.0 also encourages developing new products and business models. As a result, it modifies the workforce profile and reconfigures the competitiveness of companies and regions. These issues will be discussed later on in this chapter but first, let’s focus on the three core advancements differentiating Industry 4.0 from the previous revolutions. DATIFICATION Integrating data from devices, sensors, and IT systems enables developing new solutions at all stages of the product lifecycle – from design to production, logistics and maintenance. 1

ntinuously collecting, analysing, and using data in real-time. IIoT enables monitoring of all production processes and scheduling maintenance accordingly. When integrating Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES), Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), and Customer Relationship Management (CRM), the network allows for comprehensive management of all related operations. THE CONVERGENCE OF IT SYSTEMS AND OPERATIONAL TECHNOLOGY (OT) In the past, IT and OT worked as separate entities: the first one mostly serving management, the latter controlling machines and resources. Thanks to the IIoT, these two worlds have been increasingly converging. Cyber-physical systems (CPS) embody this tendency as machines now combine both the IT and operational qualities. One of the most advanced CP systems – Digital Twins – enables creating digital replicas of physical objects but also processes based on data collected from sensors. ROBOTISATION AND AUTOMATION Industry 4.0 is also underpinned by a growing level of robotisation and automation. Apart from automated production lines, factories now boast autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) and collaborative robots (cobots). PROJECT ID: P171305

LOAN NUMBER: IDA-68980

 

REFERENCE NUMBER: NITA-UDAP/CONS/26-27/00027

 

ASSIGNMENT TITLE: CONSULTANCY SERVICES FOR THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE NATIONAL DIGITAL SKILLS TRAINING PROGRAMME (NDSTP)

 

The Government of Uganda, represented by the National Information Technology Authority – Uganda (NITA-U), has received financing from the World Bank towards the cost of the Uganda Digital Acceleration Project – Government Network (UDAP-GOVNET) and intends to apply part of the proceeds for Consultancy services for the implementation of the National Digital Skills Training Programme (NDSTP)

 

The con

responsibility of implementation of the National Digital Skills Training Programme (NDSTP) programme across Uganda. The assignment will equip at least 6,000 beneficiaries drawn from public servants, teachers and tutors, out-of-school youth, refugees and refugee-host communities, and persons with disabilities with the digital knowledge and practical competencies needed to access services safely and productively, pursue education and livelihood opportunities, and participate as informed digital citizens.

The duration of the assignment will be five (5) months from the date of contract signing.

The detailed Terms of Reference (ToR) for the assignment can be accessed at https://www.nita.go.ug

The National Information Technology Authority - Uganda now invites eligible consulting firms to indicate their interest in providing the services. Interested Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the Services. insurance_bonds.text: EMENT OF OBJECTIVES (SOO) For Secure by-Design Space Vehicle (SDSV) Topic Area 3 1.0 Purpose The objective of this effort is to address cyber threats to national critical space missions (e.g., Position, Navigation, and Timing (PNT), Missile Warning/Missile Tracking (MW/MT), Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR), and Satellite Communications (SATCOM)) through the research, design, development, testing, and demonstration of a comprehensive Secure by-Design Space Vehicle (SDSV) system. 2.0 Background Space vehicles are increasingly recognized as vulnerable platforms facing sophisticated cyber threats. To ensure mission assurance, there is a critical need to provide advanced defensive solutions for space assets. f_Objectives_-_SOO.pdf ===== STATEMENT OF OBJECTIVES (SOO) For Secure by-Design Space Vehicle (SDSV) Topic Area 3 1.0 Purpose The objective of this effort is to address cyber threats to national critical space missions (e.g., Position, Navigation, and Timing (PNT), Missile Warning/Missile Tracking (MW/MT), Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR), and Satellite Communications (SATCOM)) through the research, design, development, testing, and demonstration of a comprehensive Secure by-Design Space Vehicle (SDSV) system. 2.0 Background Space vehicles are increasingly recognized as vulnerable platforms facing sophisticated cyber threats. To meet these ESR bunch injection schemes and requirements, an array of stripline-based kickers, individually fed by high voltage (HV) pulse signals of up to +/-30 kV, will be installed in the ESR. The required deflection angle is in the range 1- 1.5 mrad, for the individual stripline kicker we target a deflection angle of ~125 µrad @ 18 GeV, assuming +/-27 kV pulse supply voltage between the kicker electrodes. To keep the losses of the stored beam low, a ~15 σ distance between the stored beam and the injection septa in the ESR must be maintained, which translates into a minimum physical aperture of 30 mm diameter for the stripline kickers. ip_data_security.text: nboarding the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) to the National Eye Institute’s (NEI) existing OpenSpecimen biobanking software instance and implementing associated Electronic Medical Record (EMR) integration services. Competition is restricted to Krishagni LLC because NHLBI’s requirement is specifically to onboard to NEI’s active, Krishagni-licensed and operated OpenSpecimen environment rather than to procure a separate standalone biobanking system. Acquiring a different biobanking product would not satisfy the requirement to join the existing NEI shared instance and would result in substantial duplication of software licensing, implementation, validation, and support infrastructure costs, as well as unacceptable operational delays. As the software developer, proprietor, and operator of the existing NEI OpenSpecimen environment, Krishagni LLC is the only responsible source authorized and technically capable of performing the required onboarding, workflow configuration, and EMR integration services within that shared platform. Requirements/Salient Characteristics: The following specification lists the minimum requirements for a lock-in amplifier. Objective requirements are also highlighted when available. A lock-in amplifier is crucial for separating laser photodetector outputs from noise that may otherwise drown out the signal. Therefore, this lock-in component is necessary for meeting mission requirements. 3.1. The lock-in amplifier shall meet the following technical requirements: 3.1.1. Demodulation capability for DC up to 600 megahertz or higher reference signals 3.1.2. At least two analog BNC inputs 3.1.3. At least two analog BNC outputs 3.1.4. Analog to digital input conversion capability included, along with the inverse of digital to analog output conversion 3.1.5. Minimum sampling rate for input data of 1.25 giga-samples per second (GSa/s) 3.1.6. USB 2.0 or USB-C interface is supported 3.1.7. PC software interface included 3.1.8. Coding support for either Python or MATLAB languages 3.1.8.1. API for supported language must be given 3.1.9. Come with a manufacturer’s warranty of at least 1 year 3.1.10. Signal output must support digital to analog conversion of at least 1.25 giga-s
